subtopics.title: Vibrating sources: excitation, frequency and coupling to air
subtopics.learning_goal: Sound is generated by mechanical excitation of a medium by a vibrating source. Source motion, coupling, propagation and detection are distinct links in the causal chain.

Shortest valid route: Gas path weakens, source may still vibrate; support transmits structure-borne signal or other path; independently measure source motion.

science_records.claim: Sound is generated by mechanical excitation of a medium by a vibrating source. Source motion, coupling, propagation and detection are distinct links in the causal chain.
science_records.law_or_model: For periodic motion, T=Δt/N and f=1/T; a detector records the field at its location, not necessarily the source displacement.
assumptions: Periodic source model only when repetition is stable; nonperiodic pulses require other descriptors.
Microphone voltage requires calibration before pressure comparisons.
conditions_and_limits: Periodic source model only when repetition is stable; nonperiodic pulses require other descriptors.
Microphone voltage requires calibration before pressure comparisons.
Same-frequency claim assumes steady transmission and suitable detector; phase delay can be ambiguous.
A vacuum removes gas-borne sound but not necessarily solid-borne bypasses or electronic artifacts.
science_records.units_and_signs: Displacement in m or mm, time in s, f in Hz; sensor voltage is not pressure unless calibrated.

core1a.phenomenon: A vibrating ruler can remain visibly in motion while the sound reaching a listener becomes much weaker.
core1a.scientific_narrative:
A sound source is a mechanical system capable of transferring energy into its surroundings. A plucked string moves back and forth, a stretched membrane oscillates, and a vibrating reed or changing airflow can excite an air column. The disturbance moves through a material medium to a receiver. The material of the source is not carried to the listener. The source can keep vibrating even when coupling to the surrounding medium becomes weak.

A periodic source repeats its state after a period T; frequency f counts full repetitions per second. A sound that is more complicated than a sinusoid may contain multiple frequency components. A string, membrane and air column can have different mode shapes and may produce similar fundamental frequencies. Hearing a frequency does not uniquely identify an instrument or the mechanism by which it was excited. A string may be plucked, struck or bowed; similar periodic motion can result from different driving methods.

Separate the causal links: energy input causes source motion, the moving boundary excites a disturbance, the medium transports it, and the receiver converts it into a measured signal. A large source displacement need not imply a large pressure signal far away. Source area, geometry, coupling, intervening medium and detector response matter. A sensor attached to the source measures a different quantity from a microphone in air. A microphone voltage is not automatically a pressure amplitude without calibration.

To observe an oscillation, label displacement and time axes, count complete repetitions between matching phase points, and convert units. A source and receiver time trace may have the same repetition frequency with a delay if a single steady tone propagates through a stationary medium and the receiver response is suitable. A pulse envelope can establish arrival time; two periodic sinusoidal traces alone can have a phase delay ambiguous by whole periods. This distinction will be developed in PH08-04 and PH08-07. A quiet receiver signal could reflect weaker source vibration, changed coupling, propagation obstruction or a sensor fault. A controlled test keeps source motion and receiver conditions matched while varying one link.

For a source in a bell jar as air is removed, an ideal vacuum cannot carry sound through the gas path, yet mechanical vibration may continue and structure-borne sound may still travel through solid supports. Do not infer that the source stopped merely because an external microphone signal weakened. Use direct motion measurement and path controls. Avoid high sound levels in demonstrations. The current inspectable Core2 bank has no matching source-excitation question; these examples are original transfer.

derivation_steps.why_valid: They are distinct components of the causal chain.

derivation_steps.action: Measure source oscillation independently of receiver output.
derivation_steps.why_valid: A weak receiver signal alone does not establish weaker source motion.

derivation_steps.action: Count same-phase repetitions and identify the recorded variable.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Frequency is determined by repetition, not graph height.

derivation_steps.why_valid: Independent observations distinguish source change from path or sensor change.

progressive_examples.problem: A membrane completes 12 cycles in 0.06 s. Find frequency and period.
A string oscillates with unchanged measured period and displacement, but enclosing it reduces microphone output. Does this prove its frequency changed?
progressive_examples.reasoning: No. The source measurement is unchanged; enclosure may alter coupling or propagation. Check calibrated microphone and path.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Compare source traces independently of receiver output.

progressive_examples.problem: Two sensors record the same steady 250 Hz tone, with one trace apparently delayed 1 ms. Is travel delay unique?
progressive_examples.reasoning: Period 4 ms; delays 1 ms+4n ms can give the same periodic phase offset. A pulse or independent path length constrains n.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Use a timed onset, not just steady phase.

figures.scene_description: The source vibration can be measured separately from the medium and microphone; a solid support is a possible alternate path. Original inline SVG.

misconception.wrong_model: A weaker sound at the listener means the source stopped vibrating; equal frequency identifies the same instrument.
misconception.diagnostic: Can a source vibration sensor remain unchanged while a microphone output falls?
misconception.repair: Separate excitation, coupling, propagation and detection; use independent measurements.

exit_check.task: A source completes five intervals between the first and sixth matching peaks in 20 ms. Find f.

core1b.fresh_task: A motor-driven membrane has unchanged measured motion when a thick barrier is inserted between it and a microphone. Receiver signal falls. Explain the observation and propose a test separating barrier effects from microphone fault.
core1b.protected_work: Explain a receiver-signal change by tracing the source–coupling–medium–receiver chain, distinguishing vibration from transmitted sound.

stages.predict: Predict whether the reduced microphone signal establishes that the membrane itself vibrates less. Give your initial reason.
stages.attempt: A motor-driven membrane has unchanged measured motion when a thick barrier is inserted between it and a microphone. Receiver signal falls. Explain the observation and propose a test separating barrier effects from microphone fault.
stages.reconstruct: Source motion unchanged, barrier may reflect/absorb/alter path; verify microphone with known independent reference and compare barrier-in/out at matched geometry.
stages.diagnose: Find whether you inferred source motion from receiver amplitude alone or ignored a possible alternate transmission path.
stages.repair: Trace each causal link and give an independent observation to test the proposed source or transmission change.
stages.boundary_test: If the source motion later weakens as well, can the receiver signal alone isolate the barrier effect?

core1b.fresh_task: A buzzer inside a chamber remains visibly vibrating as air is removed. An external sensor still detects a small signal. Explain why this does not establish gas-borne sound in vacuum, and propose a discriminating observation.
core1b.protected_work: Explain a receiver-signal change by tracing the source–coupling–medium–receiver chain, distinguishing vibration from transmitted sound.

stages.predict: Do you initially expect visible source motion and external sound level to change together? State your judgement.
stages.attempt: A buzzer inside a chamber remains visibly vibrating as air is removed. An external sensor still detects a small signal. Explain why this does not establish gas-borne sound in vacuum, and propose a discriminating observation.
stages.reconstruct: Mechanical vibration persists; residual gas, solid supports or sensor artifact may account for signal. Control support coupling and independently measure pressure/source motion.
stages.diagnose: Find whether you inferred source motion from receiver amplitude alone or ignored a possible alternate transmission path.
stages.repair: Trace each causal link and give an independent observation to test the proposed source or transmission change.
stages.boundary_test: If all mechanical connections are isolated but the sensor still reports a signal, what alternative should be checked?

core1b.fresh_task: Source displacement maxima occur at 1,5,9 ms. Microphone voltage maxima occur at 4,8,12 ms. Independent pulse onset arrives 3 ms after emission. Draw two traces with correct physical axes; compare frequencies and distinguish measured delay from phase evidence.
core1b.protected_work: Represent source and receiver timing on separate labelled axes, retaining cycle intervals and an independent onset delay.

stages.predict: Predict whether the two recorded traces indicate equal repetition rates and whether their vertical scales can be compared directly.
stages.attempt: Source displacement maxima occur at 1,5,9 ms. Microphone voltage maxima occur at 4,8,12 ms. Independent pulse onset arrives 3 ms after emission. Draw two traces with correct physical axes; compare frequencies and distinguish measured delay from phase evidence.
stages.reconstruct: Both T=4 ms, f=250 Hz; source displacement and voltage axes distinct; independent pulse onset gives 3 ms, phase offset alone permits 3+4n ms.
stages.diagnose: Check whether you counted peaks or intervals, and whether you treated phase alignment as a unique travel time.
stages.repair: Construct the two independent axes with matching phase intervals, then compare onset evidence with possible whole-period offsets.
stages.boundary_test: If pulse onset was not measured, could the steady traces prove the delay is exactly 3 ms?

core1b.fresh_task: A membrane's successive maxima at 2,8,14 ms and a microphone's maxima at 3,9,15 ms are recorded. A separately timed onset gives 7 ms propagation. Sketch both traces and reconcile the different apparent offsets.
core1b.protected_work: Represent source and receiver timing on separate labelled axes, retaining cycle intervals and an independent onset delay.

stages.predict: Predict whether the apparent 1 ms offset contradicts the separately measured 7 ms delay.
stages.attempt: A membrane's successive maxima at 2,8,14 ms and a microphone's maxima at 3,9,15 ms are recorded. A separately timed onset gives 7 ms propagation. Sketch both traces and reconcile the different apparent offsets.
stages.reconstruct: Both T=6 ms, f≈166.7 Hz. Apparent phase offset 1 ms; 7 ms=1+6 ms, consistent. Different vertical quantities; onset constrains true delay.
stages.diagnose: Check whether you counted peaks or intervals, and whether you treated phase alignment as a unique travel time.
stages.repair: Construct the two independent axes with matching phase intervals, then compare onset evidence with possible whole-period offsets.
stages.boundary_test: If the membrane frequency changes but the sensor clock is miscalibrated, what independent measurement is needed?

core1b.fresh_task: A vibrating plate's displacement amplitude remains 2 mm. A receiver output changes from 8 to 3 units after a screen is added. A reference source at the receiver produces the same 5-unit reading before and after. Compare three explanations and specify a further test.
core1b.protected_work: Select among source, coupling and detector explanations using controlled interventions and an independent reference test.

stages.predict: Predict which explanation the unchanged reference reading will make less plausible, without deciding the final cause.
stages.attempt: A vibrating plate's displacement amplitude remains 2 mm. A receiver output changes from 8 to 3 units after a screen is added. A reference source at the receiver produces the same 5-unit reading before and after. Compare three explanations and specify a further test.
stages.reconstruct: Measured source amplitude unchanged, reference disfavors general gain change, screen alters path/coupling plausibly; compare screen removal and independent pressure/geometry. Frequency or unmeasured mode changes still possible.
stages.diagnose: Identify which observation actually tests the source, the path or the receiver; did you treat one ratio as unique evidence?
stages.repair: Write predictions for each causal model under the independent reference and intervention, retain compatible alternatives, and propose a discriminating control.
stages.boundary_test: If the reference output also falls from 5 to 2 units, how does the inference change?

stages.predict: Predict whether the two halved outputs uniquely establish a change in the reed's emitted sound.
stages.attempt: A reed vibrates at measured 300 Hz and 1 mm amplitude. Microphone reading falls from 10 to 5 after moving a panel. A calibrated check tone at that position falls from 6 to 3 too. Compare panel-path and detector-gain models and choose an additional control.
stages.reconstruct: Both halve, so a common gain or shared path change fits; measured source unchanged. Test microphone with known direct calibrated pressure while panel geometry held fixed or use second calibrated sensor; cannot isolate panel cause yet.
